Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)
- claude-security:claude-security: The Claude Security orchestrator, for use only as the main agent of a session (claude --agent claude-security:claude-security), where it runs a scan end to end and can turn its findings into targeted patch files, each verified by a panel of agents. Never dispatch it as a subagent: it cannot scan from there. When a user asks for Claude Security in a conversation, use the claude-security:claude-security skill instead. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Write, Edit, AskUserQuestion, Workflow, Workflow(claude-security:scan), TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskList, TaskUpdate, TaskOutput, TaskStop, Agent(claude-security:scan-inventory, claude-security:scan-researcher, claude-security:scan-verifier, claude-security:scan-loader, claude-security:scan-redactor, claude-security:patch-generator, claude-security:patch-verifier, claude-security:explore))
- claude-security:explore: Read-only code explorer that the plugin's other agents dispatch to map a codebase — locate files, trace how a flow is wired, find every caller of a symbol, answer "where does X happen". (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash)
- claude-security:patch-generator: Implements the fix for one finding inside a scratch workspace clone, staged for review and delivery as a patch file; dispatched by the fix job, not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Edit, Write, Agent(claude-security:explore))
- claude-security:patch-verifier: The single verifier per fix round — reviews the workspace's staged diff against the finding, runs the tests, and states the three confidence claims a patch file must earn; dispatched by the fix job, not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Agent(claude-security:explore))
- claude-security:scan-inventory: Restricted read-only repository cartographer dispatched by the Claude Security scan workflow to partition the tree into components and account for every top-level directory; not for direct invocation or vulnerability research. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep)
- claude-security:scan-loader: Restricted read-only loader dispatched by the Claude Security scan workflow to return one JSON file from the run directory; not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read)
- claude-security:scan-redactor: Restricted agent dispatched by the Claude Security scan jobs to replace the credential values in a finished scan's report files with [REDACTED]; not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read, Edit)
- claude-security:scan-researcher: Restricted read-only vulnerability researcher dispatched by the Claude Security scan workflow; not for direct invocation or general exploration. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Agent(claude-security:explore))
- claude-security:scan-verifier: Restricted read-only verifier dispatched by the Claude Security scan workflow to vote on one candidate finding; not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Agent(claude-security:explore))
- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

- claude-security:claude-security: Claude Security: scan the codebase (the whole repository or a scoped part of it), scan changes (this branch's or a pull request's diff, or one commit), or suggest patches (findings turned into targeted patch files, each verified by a panel of agents, that you apply when you choose). Use when the user asks to scan, audit or check code with Claude Security, to scan their changes with Claude Security, or to fix or patch Claude Security findings.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.

- anthropic-skills:import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.

This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:setup-writing-style: Learns how the user writes from their own sent messages and docs, and builds a voice profile so future drafts sound like them instead of generic AI. The profile is saved as the my-writing-style skill. Use when the user asks to set up, learn, or capture their writing voice, or complains that drafts sound generic or unlike them and no my-writing-style profile exists. Only for drafting text the user will send as themselves, not for Claude's own replies.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

# AGENTS.md

Moneo is an open-source personal-finance app you run on your own computer. One owner imports statements or syncs a bank, tracks accounts and wealth, plans spending, and asks about their money in chat, artifacts and voice calls.

Stack: Next.js 16 + React 19 + TypeScript. The backend is Postgres plus the open-source Supabase Auth, PostgREST and Storage services in Docker (`docker-compose.yml`). Drizzle schema, Workflow (local world) for durable jobs, Vitest and Playwright, and the Vercel AI SDK, paid by the owner's ChatGPT plan or an API key.

These are defaults. The developer's instructions override them; if a rule conflicts with the task, say so and ask.

## Non-negotiables

- **Local-first.** Everything listens on `127.0.0.1`; optional phone access is Tailscale forwarding to it (`lib/phone-access.ts`). Data leaves the machine only for services the owner set up (AI provider, Enable Banking, Scalable). New features must work fully offline from the cloud except those calls.
- **One owner, no accounts.** The proxy signs the owner in automatically; there is no sign-up or sign-in screen. Private access from the owner's own Tailscale devices needs no login; anything public must add one first.
- **Financial truth comes from code and data, never from AI guesses.** Money is integer minor units (`bigint`) with an explicit currency. The AI explains and proposes; every write it suggests is a card the owner accepts.
- **AI organization labels are the one exception to cards.** The organizer applies high- and medium-confidence category and merchant labels itself, marked as AI (`organized_by = 'ai'`), listed with every other AI decision and undoable; they never become owner rules or owner corrections. Every other AI write is a card.
- **History is kept.** Preserve source records, corrections, history and undo when changing financial data flows.
- **Open source.** No secrets, private statements or personal data in the repo (`npm run check:privacy` runs before tests and lint).

## How to work

1. **Think before coding.** State your assumptions. If a request has more than one reading, name them and ask instead of picking silently. If a simpler approach exists, say so.
2. **Simplicity first.** Write the least code that solves the problem: no speculative features, options or single-use abstractions. Prefer existing utilities and dependencies, and Zod for validating user and external input. Would a senior engineer call it overcomplicated? Then simplify.
3. **Surgical changes.** Touch only what the task needs and match the nearby style. Remove what your own change made unused; mention unrelated dead code instead of deleting it.
4. **Goal-driven.** Turn the task into checks you can run, then loop until they pass. A bug fix starts by reproducing the failure; see Tests for when that becomes a kept test. Purely visual changes get a before/after screenshot instead.

## Safety

- Never run tests or experiments against the owner's backend (`.env`, Docker project `moneo`, app on port 3000). Tests use the separate test backend below, as its QA user or disposable users they create and remove.
- Never delete the `moneo` Docker volumes (`docker compose down -v`) or drop its database: that is the owner's financial history. The test backend is disposable: `docker compose -p moneo-qa down -v` then `npm run setup -- --qa` starts it fresh.
- Never change `JWT_SECRET`, `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` or `BANK_TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY` in an existing `.env`; keys, sessions and stored bank and ChatGPT tokens stop working.
- Never commit `.env*` (except `.env.example`), `.data/`, `e2e/.auth.json` or `.qa/`.
- Only kill processes you started, or ones you verified by port and working directory. Never kill by name.
- Real AI, bank and Scalable calls cost money or count against limits (PSD2 allows about 4 background bank fetches a day). Mock them in tests unless the task is to check the real service.

## Hit every surface

Before calling a feature done, check where else it shows up:

- Pages and their mobile layout, light and dark.
- Chat tools and the system prompt in `lib/ai/provider.ts`, artifacts, and the voice call (`lib/ai/voice-*`).
- Home widgets and the command palette.
- Background jobs (`lib/scheduler.ts`, `workflows/`) and imports from files, banks and Scalable.
- The reverse path: undo, reset all data, reconnect, disconnect.
- Docs: `README.md` for anything the owner sets up or runs, the landing page in `docs/` when a headline feature or install step changes, `.env.example` for new variables. Deferred work goes in GitHub issues.

## Commands

Use npm (`package-lock.json` is authoritative).

- Install: `npm ci`
- Backend: `npm run setup` (writes `.env` secrets, starts Docker, applies migrations, creates the owner; safe to rerun)
- Dev: `npm run dev` (http://localhost:3000)
- Unit: `npm test` · Lint: `npm run lint` · Build: `npm run build` · Bundle budget: `npm run check:bundle` (after a build)
- Database: `npm run test:db` (needs the backend from `npm run setup`)
- E2E: `npm run test:e2e` (see `e2e/README.md`)
- Desktop release: push a `v*` tag matching `desktop/package.json`, then publish the drafted release (`desktop/README.md` → Releasing). Never tag or publish unasked.

## Test backend

Everything that needs a database or a running app is tested against `moneo-qa`, never the owner's setup:

- **Backend:** Docker project `moneo-qa` (ports 54521/54522), secrets in the git-ignored `.env.qa` (one shared copy in `~/.moneo/qa.env`, so every worktree uses the same stack). Create, upgrade or copy it into a new worktree with `npm run setup -- --qa`; then `npm run qa:auth` creates the QA user and saves `e2e/.auth.json`.
- **App:** `npm run qa:server` runs this checkout on http://localhost:3100 against `.env.qa`, building into `.next-qa`, with bank access off and a placeholder AI key that every provider rejects, so nothing costs money. `npm run test:e2e` starts it on its own and refuses to run against any server that would sign tests in as the owner.
- **Reset:** `npm run qa:reset` empties the QA workspace. Each spec should still set up the state it needs rather than rely on what earlier runs left behind.
- `npm run test:db` and the `supabase/tests/*.mjs` scripts read `.env.qa` only.
- A nightly run (`npm run qa:nightly`, see `e2e/README.md`) runs every spec twice and keeps the issue "Nightly browser suite is failing" up to date; fix what it lists before adding new specs.

## Project map

- `app/` — App Router pages, route handlers, server actions
- `lib/finance/` — deterministic financial logic
- `lib/ai/` — models, chat tools, ChatGPT sign-in (`chatgpt.ts`), voice
- `lib/bank/`, `lib/scalable/` — Enable Banking and Scalable Capital
- `lib/schema.ts` + `supabase/migrations/` — database schema
- `workflows/` — durable background jobs; `lib/scheduler.ts` runs the daily ones
- `docker-compose.yml`, `docker/`, `scripts/setup.mjs` — the self-hosted backend
- `e2e/` — Playwright flows; `supabase/tests/` — SQL regressions
- `desktop/` — the Electron app; `.github/workflows/desktop.yml` builds it and drafts releases
- `docs/` — the GitHub Pages landing page (https://indkhan.github.io/Moneo/); its download button reads the latest published release

## Sign-in callbacks and addresses

Each outside service sends the browser back to a different address. Keep these in mind before changing ports, hosts or remote access:

- **Sign in with ChatGPT** (`lib/ai/chatgpt.ts`): OpenAI only accepts the loopback `http://127.0.0.1:<PORT>/api/ai/chatgpt/callback`, so sign-in happens on the computer running Moneo. Tokens are stored there, so chat works from any device afterwards.
- **Enable Banking** (`lib/bank/return-listener.ts`): production apps need an `https://` redirect registered in the Enable Banking app. Moneo uses `https://localhost:3443/api/bank/callback` (a local listener with a cert from `npm run setup`), which forwards to `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL`.
- **Scalable Capital** (`lib/scalable/server.ts`): dynamic client registration with `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL/api/scalable/callback`. `localhost` registers freely; other hosts need Scalable's allowlist (it rejects `*.ts.net`).
- **Supabase** (`NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`, `127.0.0.1:54321`): only the server may call it; never send the browser there, or it breaks on other devices.
- **Phone and tablet** (`*.ts.net` through Tailscale Serve): the laptop's addresses above never change. The three logins refuse to start from a remote device (`lib/remote-device.ts`) and say to use the computer; everything else, including sync, works from there.
- **Voice** needs a secure context (https or localhost) for the microphone.

## Database changes

Add a new ordered migration in `supabase/migrations/` and keep `lib/schema.ts` aligned. Never rewrite an applied migration. `npm run setup` applies pending ones and records them in `supabase_migrations.schema_migrations`. For other Supabase CLI commands use `npx supabase ... --db-url "$SUPABASE_DB_URL"` (from `.env`).

## Tests

A test earns its place by failing when real behaviour breaks. Before writing one, name the bug it would catch.

- **Write tests for** money math, imports and undo, auth, RLS and AI scopes, concurrency, and bugs that actually happened (name the PR or issue).
- **Don't write tests that** assert UI copy or labels, grep source or migration files, mirror the implementation, or need more than about three `vi.mock`s to run. Test the `lib/` function instead.
- One test per behaviour. Don't add a test per requirement or per audit finding; if an existing test covers the failure, extend it.
- `npm test` must pass with no `.env`, no Docker and no network. Anything that needs the database is a `*.live.test.ts`.
- Use fake timers or controlled promises, never real waits. Mock AI, bank and Scalable; real calls are opt-in only.
- Browser specs are for whole user journeys, not single links or labels. Add a spec only when no existing journey can take the check.
- When you remove a feature, remove its tests. Never delete or skip a failing test just to get green: fix the cause, or ask.
- If a pointless test lands, find out why the agent wrote it and fix the guidance here.

Run the smallest relevant test while iterating. Before finishing, run `npm test`, `npm run lint` and `npm run typecheck`; add `npm run build` for app, config or build changes, and Playwright for changed user flows. CI runs the same checks on every pull request.

## Commits and pull requests

- Break the work into steps and commit each one; a big task is several commits.
- Write commit messages in plain language: what changed and why.
- Deferred work gets their issue created on github.
- Stacked PRs: before merging a PR that another open PR is based on, change the dependent PR's base to `main`; deleting the merged branch otherwise closes it.
- Long agent prompts and plans don't get committed; if guidance must persist, put the rule in AGENTS.md.

In All Code Is Slop (Except Mine) — Lauren Tan, SpaceXSI, Lauren Tan ("Potato") explains how she scaled from shipping 3,000 personal pull requests a month [00:42] to her team shipping 11,000 PRs a month without sacrificing software quality [13:34]. Her core thesis is that AI coding agents allow any developer to operate like an elite "coding machine," shifting the software engineer's primary job toward designing deterministic guardrails and verification systems so agents produce reliable code by default [01:04].

1. Core Thesis: Trust Through Environment Design
Productivity without quality loss: With coding agents, raw code volume is no longer the bottleneck; the real challenge is maintaining or improving code quality while scaling output [01:04].

Engineered trust over blind trust: Running a "software factory" relies on investing upfront in the agent's environment—a process that took Tan about six months to refine—so you can trust agents to do the right thing automatically [01:25].

2. The Inverse Pyramid of Agent Guardrails
Tan organizes environment investments into four layers, prioritizing deterministic code constraints at the bottom and minimizing natural-language instructions at the top [01:57]:

The codebase itself (Deterministic): Strong API design, clear architecture, and proactive refactoring form the primary foundation [02:04].

Static analysis and testing (Deterministic): Lint rules, type systems, compilers, and automated test suites constrain what agents can write and force good patterns by default [02:13].

Verification (Runtime and formal): Runtime checks and formal proofs uncover subtle bugs, enforce system invariants, and confirm the agent understood your actual intent [02:28].

Prose (Minimal top layer): Markdown rules, skills, and agents.md files should be kept small and reserved only for areas requiring genuine human judgment [02:42].

3. Codebase as a Garden & Concrete Engineering Rules
Inputs dictate outputs: Because the existing codebase is an agent's largest input, every agent correction should be converted into a deterministic code check rather than another line in a prompt or agents.md file [02:59].

Tending the garden: As PR velocity jumps from a handful per day to hundreds, code arrives like a continuous living stream [03:33]. Architectural constraints act as concrete foundations [04:03], whereas tech debt, workarounds, and anti-patterns act like weeds that agents immediately copy and spread—requiring engineers to keep the codebase pristine [04:25].

Banning high-nuance APIs: Tools that require deep nuance to use safely inevitably lead to agent "slop" [05:24]. In Dune (a Next.js-like client framework built for Electron apps), Tan's team banned React's useEffect in product code—allowing it only inside controlled framework APIs—which categorically eliminated a whole class of code review issues [04:58].

Enforcing architecture via directory structure: To stop agents from importing Electron main-thread code into the renderer thread (which causes UI jank) [06:15], they split code into explicit electron-renderer and electron-main top-level directories and blocked cross-imports with lint rules and a dependency graph analyzer [06:30].

Banning 99% of code comments: Agents frequently use markdown files and inline comments to rationalize hacks or over-rotate on minor feedback [07:00]. For example, an architectural mismatch between VS Code's imperative style and React's declarative style previously led agents to spam timers (setTimeout, requestAnimationFrame, requestIdleCallback), triggering heavy garbage collection lag while writing comments defending the workarounds [07:28]. Tan's team banned 99% of comments—because they go stale and cannot be enforced—and replaced them with descriptive lint errors that instruct agents to fix the root cause [08:17].

Shrinking human code review: Systematically converting review feedback into lint rules and cleaner APIs steadily removes manual review bottlenecks until agents can safely merge most of their own pull requests [09:08].

4. Verification & The Golden Age of Testing
Reviewing artifacts instead of diffs: Code review shifts toward inspecting verification artifacts such as videos, screenshots, diagrams, and formal proofs [09:44].

Runtime verification with feature maps and CLIs: Agents run and debug the app directly using tools like the Chrome DevTools Protocol [10:06]. A user-facing feature map (acting like a UI sitemap) gives agents shared vocabulary for interface components, while reusable custom CLIs inside agent skills reduce token consumption and improve reliability [10:06].

Formal verification and property-based UI testing:

TLA+: Used for model checking complex user flows, such as multi-device notifications [10:52].

Lean: Used to mathematically prove critical algorithms, such as ensuring a custom virtualization library has zero flickering or jitter [11:05].

Bombadil: Used for property-based UI testing to catch subtle interface bugs [11:40].

The economics of verification: Echoing industry observations that roughly 70% of daily tokens now go toward verification [11:51], Tan notes that agents make historically expensive testing and formal methods cheap enough to use routinely—sparking a "golden age of software testing and verification" [12:23].

Visualizing state machines: Tan built a state-chart skill (in her psac / potato stack plugin) to generate user-facing state machine diagrams that can be reviewed alongside videos and screenshots [12:59].

5. Production Results & Outer-Loop Automation
Real-world throughput and stability: Using these practices, the Graphbot team shipped 11,000 pull requests in one month, cuts daily stable releases, and onboarded 227 contributors in October—including casual contributors with minimal prior context [13:26]. Meanwhile, the PR revert rate dropped to roughly 0.5% [14:15], and core Electron app metrics (startup, typing, and chat switching) grew faster than at launch [14:31].

Fix the inner loop before automating the outer loop: Automating a sloppy coding loop only generates faster, more expensive slop [15:12]. Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)
- claude-security:claude-security: The Claude Security orchestrator, for use only as the main agent of a session (claude --agent claude-security:claude-security), where it runs a scan end to end and can turn its findings into targeted patch files, each verified by a panel of agents. Never dispatch it as a subagent: it cannot scan from there. When a user asks for Claude Security in a conversation, use the claude-security:claude-security skill instead. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Write, Edit, AskUserQuestion, Workflow, Workflow(claude-security:scan), TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskList, TaskUpdate, TaskOutput, TaskStop, Agent(claude-security:scan-inventory, claude-security:scan-researcher, claude-security:scan-verifier, claude-security:scan-loader, claude-security:scan-redactor, claude-security:patch-generator, claude-security:patch-verifier, claude-security:explore))
- claude-security:explore: Read-only code explorer that the plugin's other agents dispatch to map a codebase — locate files, trace how a flow is wired, find every caller of a symbol, answer "where does X happen". (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash)
- claude-security:patch-generator: Implements the fix for one finding inside a scratch workspace clone, staged for review and delivery as a patch file; dispatched by the fix job, not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Edit, Write, Agent(claude-security:explore))
- claude-security:patch-verifier: The single verifier per fix round — reviews the workspace's staged diff against the finding, runs the tests, and states the three confidence claims a patch file must earn; dispatched by the fix job, not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Agent(claude-security:explore))
- claude-security:scan-inventory: Restricted read-only repository cartographer dispatched by the Claude Security scan workflow to partition the tree into components and account for every top-level directory; not for direct invocation or vulnerability research. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep)
- claude-security:scan-loader: Restricted read-only loader dispatched by the Claude Security scan workflow to return one JSON file from the run directory; not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read)
- claude-security:scan-redactor: Restricted agent dispatched by the Claude Security scan jobs to replace the credential values in a finished scan's report files with [REDACTED]; not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read, Edit)
- claude-security:scan-researcher: Restricted read-only vulnerability researcher dispatched by the Claude Security scan workflow; not for direct invocation or general exploration. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Agent(claude-security:explore))
- claude-security:scan-verifier: Restricted read-only verifier dispatched by the Claude Security scan workflow to vote on one candidate finding; not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Agent(claude-security:explore))
- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. # MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

# AGENTS.md

Moneo is an open-source personal-finance app you run on your own computer. One owner imports statements or syncs a bank, tracks accounts and wealth, plans spending, and asks about their money in chat, artifacts and voice calls.

Stack: Next.js 16 + React 19 + TypeScript. The backend is Postgres plus the open-source Supabase Auth, PostgREST and Storage services in Docker (`docker-compose.yml`). Drizzle schema, Workflow (local world) for durable jobs, Vitest and Playwright, and the Vercel AI SDK, paid by the owner's ChatGPT plan or an API key.

These are defaults. The developer's instructions override them; if a rule conflicts with the task, say so and ask.

## Non-negotiables

- **Local-first.** Everything listens on `127.0.0.1`; optional phone access is Tailscale forwarding to it (`lib/phone-access.ts`). Data leaves the machine only for services the owner set up (AI provider, Enable Banking, Scalable). New features must work fully offline from the cloud except those calls.
- **One owner, no accounts.** The proxy signs the owner in automatically; there is no sign-up or sign-in screen. Private access from the owner's own Tailscale devices needs no login; anything public must add one first.
- **Financial truth comes from code and data, never from AI guesses.** Money is integer minor units (`bigint`) with an explicit currency. The AI explains and proposes; every write it suggests is a card the owner accepts.
- **AI organization labels are the one exception to cards.** The organizer applies high- and medium-confidence category and merchant labels itself, marked as AI (`organized_by = 'ai'`), listed with every other AI decision and undoable; they never become owner rules or owner corrections. Every other AI write is a card.
- **History is kept.** Preserve source records, corrections, history and undo when changing financial data flows.
- **Open source.** No secrets, private statements or personal data in the repo (`npm run check:privacy` runs before tests and lint).

## How to work

1. **Think before coding.** State your assumptions. If a request has more than one reading, name them and ask instead of picking silently. If a simpler approach exists, say so.
2. **Simplicity first.** Write the least code that solves the problem: no speculative features, options or single-use abstractions. Prefer existing utilities and dependencies, and Zod for validating user and external input. Would a senior engineer call it overcomplicated? Then simplify.
3. **Surgical changes.** Touch only what the task needs and match the nearby style. Remove what your own change made unused; mention unrelated dead code instead of deleting it.
4. **Goal-driven.** Turn the task into checks you can run, then loop until they pass. A bug fix starts by reproducing the failure; see Tests for when that becomes a kept test. Purely visual changes get a before/after screenshot instead.

## Safety

- Never run tests or experiments against the owner's backend (`.env`, Docker project `moneo`, app on port 3000). Tests use the separate test backend below, as its QA user or disposable users they create and remove.
- Never delete the `moneo` Docker volumes (`docker compose down -v`) or drop its database: that is the owner's financial history. The test backend is disposable: `docker compose -p moneo-qa down -v` then `npm run setup -- --qa` starts it fresh.
- Never change `JWT_SECRET`, `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` or `BANK_TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY` in an existing `.env`; keys, sessions and stored bank and ChatGPT tokens stop working.
- Never commit `.env*` (except `.env.example`), `.data/`, `e2e/.auth.json` or `.qa/`.
- Only kill processes you started, or ones you verified by port and working directory. Never kill by name.
- Real AI, bank and Scalable calls cost money or count against limits (PSD2 allows about 4 background bank fetches a day). Mock them in tests unless the task is to check the real service.

## Hit every surface

Before calling a feature done, check where else it shows up:

- Pages and their mobile layout, light and dark.
- Chat tools and the system prompt in `lib/ai/provider.ts`, artifacts, and the voice call (`lib/ai/voice-*`).
- Home widgets and the command palette.
- Background jobs (`lib/scheduler.ts`, `workflows/`) and imports from files, banks and Scalable.
- The reverse path: undo, reset all data, reconnect, disconnect.
- Docs: `README.md` for anything the owner sets up or runs, the landing page in `docs/` when a headline feature or install step changes, `.env.example` for new variables. Deferred work goes in GitHub issues.

## Commands

Use npm (`package-lock.json` is authoritative).

- Install: `npm ci`
- Backend: `npm run setup` (writes `.env` secrets, starts Docker, applies migrations, creates the owner; safe to rerun)
- Dev: `npm run dev` (http://localhost:3000)
- Unit: `npm test` · Lint: `npm run lint` · Build: `npm run build` · Bundle budget: `npm run check:bundle` (after a build)
- Database: `npm run test:db` (needs the backend from `npm run setup`)
- E2E: `npm run test:e2e` (see `e2e/README.md`)
- Desktop release: push a `v*` tag matching `desktop/package.json`, then publish the drafted release (`desktop/README.md` → Releasing). Never tag or publish unasked.

## Test backend

Everything that needs a database or a running app is tested against `moneo-qa`, never the owner's setup:

- **Backend:** Docker project `moneo-qa` (ports 54521/54522), secrets in the git-ignored `.env.qa` (one shared copy in `~/.moneo/qa.env`, so every worktree uses the same stack). Create, upgrade or copy it into a new worktree with `npm run setup -- --qa`; then `npm run qa:auth` creates the QA user and saves `e2e/.auth.json`.
- **App:** `npm run qa:server` runs this checkout on http://localhost:3100 against `.env.qa`, building into `.next-qa`, with bank access off and a placeholder AI key that every provider rejects, so nothing costs money. `npm run test:e2e` starts it on its own and refuses to run against any server that would sign tests in as the owner.
- **Reset:** `npm run qa:reset` empties the QA workspace. Each spec should still set up the state it needs rather than rely on what earlier runs left behind.
- `npm run test:db` and the `supabase/tests/*.mjs` scripts read `.env.qa` only.
- A nightly run (`npm run qa:nightly`, see `e2e/README.md`) runs every spec twice and keeps the issue "Nightly browser suite is failing" up to date; fix what it lists before adding new specs.

## Project map

- `app/` — App Router pages, route handlers, server actions
- `lib/finance/` — deterministic financial logic
- `lib/ai/` — models, chat tools, ChatGPT sign-in (`chatgpt.ts`), voice
- `lib/bank/`, `lib/scalable/` — Enable Banking and Scalable Capital
- `lib/schema.ts` + `supabase/migrations/` — database schema
- `workflows/` — durable background jobs; `lib/scheduler.ts` runs the daily ones
- `docker-compose.yml`, `docker/`, `scripts/setup.mjs` — the self-hosted backend
- `e2e/` — Playwright flows; `supabase/tests/` — SQL regressions
- `desktop/` — the Electron app; `.github/workflows/desktop.yml` builds it and drafts releases
- `docs/` — the GitHub Pages landing page (https://indkhan.github.io/Moneo/); its download button reads the latest published release

## Sign-in callbacks and addresses

Each outside service sends the browser back to a different address. Keep these in mind before changing ports, hosts or remote access:

- **Sign in with ChatGPT** (`lib/ai/chatgpt.ts`): OpenAI only accepts the loopback `http://127.0.0.1:<PORT>/api/ai/chatgpt/callback`, so sign-in happens on the computer running Moneo. Tokens are stored there, so chat works from any device afterwards.
- **Enable Banking** (`lib/bank/return-listener.ts`): production apps need an `https://` redirect registered in the Enable Banking app. Moneo uses `https://localhost:3443/api/bank/callback` (a local listener with a cert from `npm run setup`), which forwards to `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL`.
- **Scalable Capital** (`lib/scalable/server.ts`): dynamic client registration with `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL/api/scalable/callback`. `localhost` registers freely; other hosts need Scalable's allowlist (it rejects `*.ts.net`).
- **Supabase** (`NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`, `127.0.0.1:54321`): only the server may call it; never send the browser there, or it breaks on other devices.
- **Phone and tablet** (`*.ts.net` through Tailscale Serve): the laptop's addresses above never change. The three logins refuse to start from a remote device (`lib/remote-device.ts`) and say to use the computer; everything else, including sync, works from there.
- **Voice** needs a secure context (https or localhost) for the microphone.

## Database changes

Add a new ordered migration in `supabase/migrations/` and keep `lib/schema.ts` aligned. Never rewrite an applied migration. `npm run setup` applies pending ones and records them in `supabase_migrations.schema_migrations`. For other Supabase CLI commands use `npx supabase ... --db-url "$SUPABASE_DB_URL"` (from `.env`).

## Tests

A test earns its place by failing when real behaviour breaks. Before writing one, name the bug it would catch.

- **Write tests for** money math, imports and undo, auth, RLS and AI scopes, concurrency, and bugs that actually happened (name the PR or issue).
- **Don't write tests that** assert UI copy or labels, grep source or migration files, mirror the implementation, or need more than about three `vi.mock`s to run. Test the `lib/` function instead.
- One test per behaviour. Don't add a test per requirement or per audit finding; if an existing test covers the failure, extend it.
- `npm test` must pass with no `.env`, no Docker and no network. Anything that needs the database is a `*.live.test.ts`.
- Use fake timers or controlled promises, never real waits. Mock AI, bank and Scalable; real calls are opt-in only.
- Browser specs are for whole user journeys, not single links or labels. Add a spec only when no existing journey can take the check.
- When you remove a feature, remove its tests. Never delete or skip a failing test just to get green: fix the cause, or ask.
- If a pointless test lands, find out why the agent wrote it and fix the guidance here.

Run the smallest relevant test while iterating. Before finishing, run `npm test`, `npm run lint` and `npm run typecheck`; add `npm run build` for app, config or build changes, and Playwright for changed user flows. CI runs the same checks on every pull request.

## Commits and pull requests

- Break the work into steps and commit each one; a big task is several commits.
- Write commit messages in plain language: what changed and why.
- Deferred work gets their issue created on github.
- Stacked PRs: before merging a PR that another open PR is based on, change the dependent PR's base to `main`; deleting the merged branch otherwise closes it.
- Long agent prompts and plans don't get committed; if guidance must persist, put the rule in AGENTS.md.
- suggest edits in agents.md if there was something that is changed or needs to be there in agents.md but only suggest when it is actually needed dont suggest just for suggesting.(only for prs)

In All Code Is Slop (Except Mine) — Lauren Tan, SpaceXSI, Lauren Tan ("Potato") explains how she scaled from shipping 3,000 personal pull requests a month [00:42] to her team shipping 11,000 PRs a month without sacrificing software quality [13:34]. Her core thesis is that AI coding agents allow any developer to operate like an elite "coding machine," shifting the software engineer's primary job toward designing deterministic guardrails and verification systems so agents produce reliable code by default [01:04].

1. Core Thesis: Trust Through Environment Design
Productivity without quality loss: With coding agents, raw code volume is no longer the bottleneck; the real challenge is maintaining or improving code quality while scaling output [01:04].

Engineered trust over blind trust: Running a "software factory" relies on investing upfront in the agent's environment—a process that took Tan about six months to refine—so you can trust agents to do the right thing automatically [01:25].

2. The Inverse Pyramid of Agent Guardrails
Tan organizes environment investments into four layers, prioritizing deterministic code constraints at the bottom and minimizing natural-language instructions at the top [01:57]:

The codebase itself (Deterministic): Strong API design, clear architecture, and proactive refactoring form the primary foundation [02:04].

Static analysis and testing (Deterministic): Lint rules, type systems, compilers, and automated test suites constrain what agents can write and force good patterns by default [02:13].

Verification (Runtime and formal): Runtime checks and formal proofs uncover subtle bugs, enforce system invariants, and confirm the agent understood your actual intent [02:28].

Prose (Minimal top layer): Markdown rules, skills, and agents.md files should be kept small and reserved only for areas requiring genuine human judgment [02:42].

3. Codebase as a Garden & Concrete Engineering Rules
Inputs dictate outputs: Because the existing codebase is an agent's largest input, every agent correction should be converted into a deterministic code check rather than another line in a prompt or agents.md file [02:59].

Tending the garden: As PR velocity jumps from a handful per day to hundreds, code arrives like a continuous living stream [03:33]. Architectural constraints act as concrete foundations [04:03], whereas tech debt, workarounds, and anti-patterns act like weeds that agents immediately copy and spread—requiring engineers to keep the codebase pristine [04:25].

Banning high-nuance APIs: Tools that require deep nuance to use safely inevitably lead to agent "slop" [05:24]. In Dune (a Next.js-like client framework built for Electron apps), Tan's team banned React's useEffect in product code—allowing it only inside controlled framework APIs—which categorically eliminated a whole class of code review issues [04:58].

Enforcing architecture via directory structure: To stop agents from importing Electron main-thread code into the renderer thread (which causes UI jank) [06:15], they split code into explicit electron-renderer and electron-main top-level directories and blocked cross-imports with lint rules and a dependency graph analyzer [06:30].

Banning 99% of code comments: Agents frequently use markdown files and inline comments to rationalize hacks or over-rotate on minor feedback [07:00]. For example, an architectural mismatch between VS Code's imperative style and React's declarative style previously led agents to spam timers (setTimeout, requestAnimationFrame, requestIdleCallback), triggering heavy garbage collection lag while writing comments defending the workarounds [07:28]. Tan's team banned 99% of comments—because they go stale and cannot be enforced—and replaced them with descriptive lint errors that instruct agents to fix the root cause [08:17].

Shrinking human code review: Systematically converting review feedback into lint rules and cleaner APIs steadily removes manual review bottlenecks until agents can safely merge most of their own pull requests [09:08].

4. Verification & The Golden Age of Testing
Reviewing artifacts instead of diffs: Code review shifts toward inspecting verification artifacts such as videos, screenshots, diagrams, and formal proofs [09:44].

Runtime verification with feature maps and CLIs: Agents run and debug the app directly using tools like the Chrome DevTools Protocol [10:06]. A user-facing feature map (acting like a UI sitemap) gives agents shared vocabulary for interface components, while reusable custom CLIs inside agent skills reduce token consumption and improve reliability [10:06].

Formal verification and property-based UI testing:

TLA+: Used for model checking complex user flows, such as multi-device notifications [10:52].

Lean: Used to mathematically prove critical algorithms, such as ensuring a custom virtualization library has zero flickering or jitter [11:05].

Bombadil: Used for property-based UI testing to catch subtle interface bugs [11:40].

The economics of verification: Echoing industry observations that roughly 70% of daily tokens now go toward verification [11:51], Tan notes that agents make historically expensive testing and formal methods cheap enough to use routinely—sparking a "golden age of software testing and verification" [12:23].

Visualizing state machines: Tan built a state-chart skill (in her psac / potato stack plugin) to generate user-facing state machine diagrams that can be reviewed alongside videos and screenshots [12:59].

5. Production Results & Outer-Loop Automation
Real-world throughput and stability: Using these practices, the Graphbot team shipped 11,000 pull requests in one month, cuts daily stable releases, and onboarded 227 contributors in October—including casual contributors with minimal prior context [13:26]. Meanwhile, the PR revert rate dropped to roughly 0.5% [14:15], and core Electron app metrics (startup, typing, and chat switching) grew faster than at launch [14:31].

Fix the inner loop before automating the outer loop: Automating a sloppy coding loop only generates faster, more expensive slop [15:12]. Once static checks and verification foundations are solid, teams can orchestrate outer-loop automation—such as automatically spinning up Cursor cloud agents on every new release to fuzz the build like a real user, open fix PRs, and automerge them [16:07].
